meta.name: How to Teach a Dog Recall: A Step-by-Step Plan for Coming When Called
meta.title_tag: How to Teach a Dog Recall (Come When Called)
meta.excerpt: A reliable recall is built, not commanded. This step-by-step plan takes you from a fresh cue in the kitchen to coming away from squirrels, with the games, rewards, long-line setup and fixes that keep it working, including through the teenage months.
meta.meta_description: Teach your dog to come when called: pick a cue, build it indoors, move to a long line, add distractions slowly, and fix a recall that has stopped working.
meta.author: Kailun Zhang

hero.alt: Young dog running toward the camera on a long training line — practicing recall

body_html:
Quick Answer: Pick one fresh cue, say it once, and pay with real food every time. Build it indoors first, then add distance and distractions, then practice outside on a long line clipped to a harness (AKC; VCA). Never repeat the cue, chase your dog or call them for something unpleasant (AKC). Expect a wobble in the teenage months (Asher et al., 2020), and go off leash only where it’s safe and legal. Step-by-step plan ↓

What a Reliable Recall Really Means

Every recall asks your dog to leave something interesting (AKC), so make coming to you the best deal on offer. AKC calls a recall reliable when you’re 99.99% sure your dog will come, enthusiastically; it’s never guaranteed. It matters most in emergencies, such as a squirrel near traffic or wildlife on the trail (AKC; BC SPCA).

Before You Start: Your Cue, Your Rewards and Your Gear

Pick one cue and protect it

If “come” has been repeated and ignored for months, it may be a poisoned cue, a word that has lost its meaning. Switch to a new one, such as “here” or “close,” retrain from scratch, and get the whole household using it the same way (AKC). Save it for practice and real need; use a casual phrase such as “over here” around the house (AKC).

Pay with food your dog loves

Praise alone is weak pay for most dogs. In lab tests, food beat brief social interaction as a reward (Feuerbacher & Wynne, 2012), and spoken praise drew little more interest than no interaction, though petting did better (Feuerbacher & Wynne, 2015). But in a brain-imaging study, 13 of 15 dogs’ reward areas responded as much or more to praise as to food (Cook et al., 2016). In practice, use what your dog would leave a squirrel for, such as chicken, cheese, freeze-dried liver or a game of tug, and keep treats coming for about 30 seconds after a recall (AKC).

Gear: a long line on a harness

Outdoors, use a long line of 15 to 20 feet, or work up from a 6-foot leash to a 20- or 30-foot line (AKC). Clip it to a well-fitted body harness, never a collar or head halter: a dog that hits the end of a long line at a run gets a hard jolt. VCA’s veterinary behaviorists say never to use a head collar with a long line, and note that a harness puts minimal pressure on delicate tissue. In a neck-model test, no collar kept pressure low enough to rule out injury during pulling (Carter et al., 2020). Harnesses aren’t risk-free either: they can change how some dogs move, and injury research on all equipment is thin (Ridgway, 2026). Pick one that doesn’t rub behind the elbows (VCA). Don’t wrap the line around your hand or let it tangle underfoot; leash injuries to people usually involve tripping or entanglement (Ridgway, 2026). Check local rules too; long lines exceed the 6-foot limit in US national parks (36 CFR §2.15).

How to Teach a Dog to Come When Called, Step by Step

Start with two foundation games (AKC). In the name game, say your dog’s name once; when they look at you, mark with “yes” and treat. In “gotcha,” take hold of the collar or harness while your dog nibbles a treat, then hand it over, so being caught predicts something good. Then work through these stages in short daily sessions (AKC):

StageWhereWhat to doMove on when
1Indoors, on leash, a few feet awaySay the name, then your cue. Clap or back away; mark and reward generously on arrival.Comes every time you call
2Indoors, farther, then off leash in a quiet roomCall from the end of the leash, then off leash while running backward. Change rooms; add a sit on arrival and an occasional “gotcha.”Runs to you happily anywhere in the house
3Indoors, with distractionsStart small (another pet, someone cooking), then build up.Comes on the first call
4Outdoors, quiet spot, 6-foot leash, then long lineRepeat stages 1 and 2, letting out more line gradually.Comes on the first call from the end of the line
5Outdoors, long line, real distractionsCall mid-sniff or mid-play, reward, then release your dog to go back to it.Turns away from real distractions on one call

If you have to repeat the cue, the setting is too hard. Drop back a stage, since rushing makes a recall less reliable (AKC).

Recall Games That Build Speed

  • Catch Me: on leash, get your dog’s attention, run a few steps away as you give the cue, then stop and reward (AKC).
  • Find Me: hide in another room and call (AKC). Our indoor activities for high-energy dogs have more ideas.
  • Hot Potato: two or more people take turns calling; only the caller rewards (AKC).
  • Pay the check-ins: whenever your dog looks at you or chooses to be near you, praise and treat (AKC).

Mistakes That Quietly Break a Recall

  • Repeating the cue. “Come! Come! COME!” teaches your dog the word means the fourth time, or nothing (AKC).
  • Calling only when fun ends. If recall always means leash on and home, your dog learns to dodge it. Call during play, reward and send your dog back to play (AKC).
  • Calling for bad things. For a bath, nail trim or medicine, go and get your dog instead (AKC).
  • Scolding on arrival. Even if your dog dawdled or just chewed your shoe, praise the recall; otherwise the scolding gets linked to coming to you (AKC).

Why a Shock Collar Is Not the Shortcut

Recall is the most common reason owners use remote shock collars (AVSAB). One UK trial of 63 dogs referred for recall or off-lead problems, reported in two papers, put them to the test:

  • 92% of owners reported improvement, with no difference in results between groups, but e-collar dogs spent more time tense, yawned more and explored less than reward-trained dogs, though cortisol didn’t differ (Cooper et al., 2014).
  • Reward-focused trainers got more responses to “come” and “sit” after a single cue, and faster ones, than e-collar trainers. The authors found no evidence that e-collar training is necessary, even for recall (China et al., 2020).

The trial was small, but neither analysis found an advantage for shock. AVSAB advises against shock, prong and choke collars, and VCA’s veterinary behaviorists note that dogs quickly learn to fear a shock collar’s warning tone too.

Breed, Age and Individual Differences

Breed matters on average: across more than 14,000 dogs from 101 breeds, trainability and chasing were among the most heritable differences between breeds (MacLean et al., 2019). But in a study of 18,385 dogs, breed explained just 9% of behavioral variation between individuals (Morrill et al., 2022), so train the dog in front of you. Hounds and terriers are single-minded in pursuit, a Greyhound should be leashed outdoors or in a safely fenced yard, and once a Whippet has something to chase, nothing stops it (AKC). See our Greyhound, Whippet and Beagle puppy checklists.

Recall in the teenage months

Cornell lists ignoring you when you call as a typical teenage change. In guide-dog puppies, main carers rated trainability, a scale that includes responding to recall off lead, lower at 8 months than at 5 or 12 months (Asher et al., 2020). The dip was temporary, though pet dogs may differ. If your teenager’s recall slips, keep the long line on, drop back a stage and raise the pay (AKC); easy cues like a sit or nose touch help regain attention (Cornell). Our dog teenage phase guide has more.

What to Do When Your Dog Does Not Come

  • Don’t repeat the cue or chase. Run the other way so your dog chases you (AKC).
  • Be exciting. Clap, pat your legs or make kissy noises; an angry or boring voice gives your dog no reason to come (AKC).
  • On a long line, don’t reel your dog in. Gather the line as you walk closer, then try again (AKC).
  • If your dog is loose and nothing is urgent, walk up calmly, show a treat, take the collar and reward (AKC).
  • When your dog arrives, however slowly, be glad, then make the next session easier (AKC).

Add an emergency recall

BC SPCA trainer Saundra Clow recommends a second cue, a special word or a whistle, kept for real emergencies. Pair it with a big handful of chicken or cheese once a day for at least 7 days indoors, then on a long line outdoors, then once or twice a week long term. If you wouldn’t bet $100 your dog will come, don’t use it yet (BC SPCA).

Is Your Dog Ready to Be Off Leash?

No dog ever has to be off leash; keeping yours leashed while you train is the responsible choice (AKC). Before you unclip, check that:

  • The recall holds. Your dog comes on the first call, away from real distractions, on a long line, and happily lets you take the collar (AKC).
  • It’s legal. Leash laws can apply even in an unfenced front yard, and parks set their own rules (AKC). US national parks require a leash no longer than 6 feet, or other physical confinement, at all times (36 CFR §2.15).
  • It’s safe. A dog is only completely safe off leash where it can’t meet a car or get lost (AKC).
  • It suits your dog. Some dogs with strong prey drive should never be fully trusted off leash (AKC).

No dog is 100% reliable, so start in fenced areas (AKC). Our East Bay off-leash park guide shows which parks are fenced.

Written by Kailun Zhang, who is not a veterinarian or certified dog trainer. This guide summarizes the sources listed below. If you’re stuck, look for a certified, reward-based trainer (AVSAB) through the CCPDT or IAABC directories.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to teach a dog a reliable recall?

There’s no fixed timeline. Practice daily and raise the difficulty slowly, since rushing makes a recall less reliable (AKC). An emergency cue alone gets at least 7 days of indoor practice before going outside (BC SPCA), and teenage dogs may need extra patience (Asher et al., 2020).

What is the best recall word for a dog?

Any short word you’ll use consistently and won’t overuse. If “come” is worn out, try “here” or “close” (AKC). A whistle suits an emergency recall because it carries and sounds the same every time (BC SPCA).

Why does my dog come inside but not at the park?

Outside, every recall asks your dog to leave smells, dogs and squirrels (AKC). Even a dog that’s perfect indoors needs to restart outdoors on a 6-foot leash, then a long line (AKC).

Should I use a shock collar to teach recall?

No. In a UK trial of 63 dogs with off-lead problems, reward-focused trainers got better and faster single-cue responses to “come” than e-collar trainers, and e-collar dogs showed more signs of stress (Cooper et al., 2014; China et al., 2020). AVSAB advises against shock collars.

My dog’s recall used to be great. Why did it stop working?

Often the cue has been worn out by repetition, or recalls have ended the fun or led to something unpleasant (AKC). Adolescence plays a part too: carers rated guide-dog puppies’ trainability, including off-lead recall, lower at 8 months than at 5 or 12 months (Asher et al., 2020). Drop back a stage and raise the pay (AKC). If the change is sudden or your dog seems stiff or slow, see your vet; pain featured in about a third of referred behavior cases in one review (Mills et al., 2020).

Can every dog be trusted off leash?

No. No recall is 100% reliable, and some dogs with strong prey drive, especially hounds and terriers, should never be fully trusted off leash (AKC). Leash laws apply too; US national parks require a leash no longer than 6 feet (36 CFR §2.15).
